### The Core Question: What Is Your Primary Contribution?

If there is one question that determines which track is right for your paper, it is this: **What is the main thing you are contributing to the research community?** Not everything your paper contains. Every good paper contains many things. Rather, ask yourself what is the single most valuable artifact or finding that a reader walks away with. Is it:

- **A new algorithm, method, theory, or empirical finding?** → Research track
- **A new dataset, benchmark, evaluation tool, or data curation methodology?** → Datasets & Benchmarks track
- **A working software system that others can download, install, and use?** → System Demo track

This might sound like a simplistic test, but it is the foundational question that organizers, reviewers, and area chairs use to judge whether a paper has been submitted to the right venue. Many papers contain elements of all three. A researcher who builds a benchmark often also writes code (a system) and proposes a novel evaluation methodology (an algorithm). A system demo paper frequently introduces a new dataset that the system generates. A research paper that proposes a new training algorithm will release both code and an evaluation dataset. The question is not whether your work *touches* multiple categories, but which category captures the *primary value* of your contribution.

Let us make this concrete with Dr. Chen's work. She has three outputs from her fourteen-month research project:

1. **A multilingual reasoning benchmark:** 15,000 hand-annotated questions across 40 languages, with a formal evaluation protocol, quality-controlled annotations, and inter-annotator agreement metrics. The value of this artifact is that it enables the research community to evaluate multilingual reasoning capabilities in a way that no existing benchmark does.

2. **A novel scoring algorithm:** A new metric for assessing multilingual reasoning quality that correlates better with human judgments than existing metrics like BLEU, METEOR, or BERTScore for reasoning tasks. The value of this artifact is the algorithmic innovation itself: a new way to measure something.

3. **A web-based annotation tool:** A Gradio interface she built for crowd-sourcing annotations, with quality control dashboards, annotator management, and real-time agreement monitoring. The value of this artifact is the *software system* that other researchers could use for their own annotation campaigns.

Each output maps to a different track. The benchmark is a D&B contribution. The scoring algorithm is a Research contribution. The annotation tool is a potential System Demo contribution. Combining all three into one paper would mean each contribution receives only a third of the page budget. It would also be reviewed by the wrong criteria. Algorithm reviewers would ask "Where is the novelty?" about the benchmark, while dataset reviewers would ask "Where is the documentation?" about the algorithm. Your paper would compete against submissions that are laser-focused on a single contribution type. Splitting the work into targeted submissions actually *increases* both your publication count and the impact of each paper. Each one will be reviewed by an audience that understands and values its specific type of contribution.

### The Three Tracks Compared

The following table provides a detailed comparison across the dimensions that matter most when choosing a track. Study it carefully: it condenses information from multiple calls for papers and reviewer guidelines into a single unified view.

| Dimension | Research Track | D&B Track | System Demo Track |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary contribution** | Novel algorithm, method, theory, or empirical finding | Novel dataset, benchmark, evaluation tool, or data curation practice | Working software system with demonstrable usability |
| **The core reviewer question** | "Does this advance the state of the art?" | "Will this dataset/benchmark be useful to the community?" | "Does this system work and is it usable?" |
| **Novelty expectation** | Algorithmic or theoretical novelty required | Data novelty OR methodological novelty in curation/evaluation design | Novelty in system design, integration, or utility  |
| **Evaluation approach** | Beat SOTA on existing benchmarks; ablation studies | Demonstrate dataset quality; run baseline experiments on new benchmark | User studies, adoption metrics, case studies |
| **Blind review** | Double-blind (NeurIPS, ACL/EMNLP) | Single-blind (NeurIPS, KDD) | Single-blind (*CL venues) |
| **Page limits** | 8–9 pages (NeurIPS, ACL) | 9 pages (NeurIPS), 8 pages (KDD) | 6 pages (*CL venues) |
| **Required artifacts** | Code (encouraged), reproducibility checklist | Hosted dataset + Croissant metadata (NeurIPS 2025), code, documentation | Demo video (2–2.5 min), live demo URL, screenshots |
| **What gets desk-rejected** | Anonymity violations (double-blind) | Dataset not accessible at review time (NeurIPS 2025) | No video, no working demo |
| **Typical acceptance rate** | ~25–30% (NeurIPS main), ~20–25% (ACL main) | ~36% (NeurIPS D&B, 2022) | ~32–36% (ACL/EMNLP demos) |

Several details in this table deserve unpacking.

**Single-blind vs. double-blind.** The D&B track at NeurIPS is single-blind. Reviewers can see who the authors are. This is a deliberate choice, not a lapse. Unlike algorithm papers, where intellectual contribution can be assessed from the text alone, D&B papers require reviewers to verify that the data is accessible, that the hosting is reliable, and that the claimed quality controls were implemented. If an author says "our dataset is hosted on HuggingFace with Croissant metadata," the reviewer can check. Anonymizing this would hide important verifiable claims. KDD's D&B track is also single-blind. System Demo papers at *CL venues are single-blind for similar reasons. Reviewers need to test the live demo and evaluate the video. Only the main research tracks maintain double-blind review.

**Page limits and page strategy.** The D&B and Research tracks at NeurIPS both allow 9 pages of content (plus unlimited appendices and references). This means D&B papers have the same real estate as research papers. This was a deliberate decision when the track was created. Giving D&B papers the same space signals that they are valued equally. However, the *allocation* within those 9 pages differs dramatically. A research paper might spend 3–4 pages on the method and 2–3 pages on experiments. A dataset paper might spend 3–4 pages on the data collection process and documentation, and 1–2 pages on baseline experiments. The page budget reflects the contribution type. System Demo papers at *CL venues, by contrast, have only 6 pages. This tighter constraint demands ruthless prioritization.

**Required artifacts escalation.** The NeurIPS D&B track has progressively tightened its artifact requirements. In 2021, dataset accessibility was encouraged. In 2022, it was expected. By 2025, it is mandatory: papers must provide a hosted dataset on an approved platform (HuggingFace, Kaggle, OpenML, Dataverse) with Croissant metadata, and non-compliance can result in desk rejection. This escalation reflects a maturation of the track. Early years were about establishing legitimacy; later years are about raising quality bars.


### The Artifact vs. Knowledge Distinction

The ACL Rolling Review (ARR) reviewer tutorial introduces a framework that elegantly captures the difference between these tracks. It distinguishes between two types of research contributions:

**Knowledge contributions** are things you *learn* from reading the paper. A new algorithm, a theoretical proof, an empirical finding that changes how you think about a problem: these are knowledge contributions. The value exists in the *ideas*, and once you understand them, you could in principle recreate the work. Research papers are primarily knowledge contributions.

**Artifact contributions** are things you *download and use*. A dataset, a benchmark, a software library, an annotation tool: these are artifact contributions. The value exists in the *thing itself*, and reading about it is not a substitute for having it. D&B papers and System Demo papers are both artifact contributions.

This distinction is powerful because it explains *why* the review criteria differ. For a knowledge contribution, the reviewer asks: "Is this idea novel? Is it correct? Is it significant?" For an artifact contribution, the reviewer asks: "Is this thing high-quality? Is it accessible? Is it well-documented? Will people actually use it?" These are fundamentally different evaluation frameworks, and applying the wrong one leads to unfair reviews.

The difference between D&B and System Demo within the artifact category is *what kind of artifact*:

- **D&B papers** contribute *data and evaluation infrastructure*: datasets you train on or evaluate against, benchmarks you report scores on, evaluation metrics you compute with, data quality tools you audit with
- **System Demo papers** contribute *software systems*: tools you install and interact with, libraries you import and call, platforms you log into and use through a UI

There are gray areas (a dataset generation *tool* could be either), but the intent is usually clear from the paper's emphasis. If the paper spends most of its pages describing the *data* that the tool produces, its quality, its documentation, and its baselines, it is a D&B paper that happens to include a tool. If the paper spends most of its pages describing the *system* (its architecture, its user interface, its design goals, its adoption), it is a System Demo paper that happens to produce data.


### Where Papers Fall: Real Examples

Theory is helpful, but worked examples are better. Let us trace through several well-known papers and identify which track they belong to, and why.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Why was SWE-bench published in the research track at ICLR, not a D&B track?"}
SWE-bench is a benchmark. It defines a task (resolve real GitHub issues), provides evaluation infrastructure (a Docker-based harness that runs test suites), and tests AI systems on real-world software engineering challenges. By all definitions, it is a D&B contribution. Yet it was published in the ICLR 2024 main research track, not a D&B track (ICLR does not have one). This highlights an important practical reality: not every venue has a D&B track. At venues without one (ICLR, ACL, EMNLP), dataset and benchmark papers compete in the main track. ACL and EMNLP have addressed this by explicitly instructing reviewers to value dataset papers equally and not penalize them for lacking algorithmic novelty. ICLR has no such explicit guidance, but SWE-bench was accepted because the paper also introduced an initial agent (SWE-agent) and provided substantial experimental evaluation. This effectively made the paper a hybrid. At NeurIPS, it would have been a natural fit for the D&B track.
:::

| Paper | Track | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **LAION-5B** ([Schuhmann et al., NeurIPS 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08402)) | D&B | The contribution is the 5.85 billion image-text pair dataset itself. No new model is proposed. The paper's value is that it provides large-scale training data for vision-language models. It enabled Stable Diffusion. |
| **PRISM Alignment Dataset** ([Kirk et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16019)) | D&B | The contribution is a participatory dataset from 75 countries for studying multicultural LLM alignment. The insight is in the *data design* (who was asked, how preferences were collected, what cultural patterns emerge), not in a new RLHF algorithm. |
| **ClimSim** ([Yu et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08754)) | D&B | The contribution is 5.7 billion multivariate pairs for hybrid physics-ML climate emulation. This is the first large-scale dataset bridging climate science and ML. Cross-disciplinary dataset that opened a new research direction. |
| **DecodingTrust** ([Wang et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11698)) | D&B | The contribution is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating GPT's trustworthiness across toxicity, bias, privacy, and robustness. The benchmark *framework* is the innovation, not any specific model evaluation result. |
| **SWE-bench** ([Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)) | Research (hybrid) | Benchmark + initial SWE-agent results. Could have been D&B at NeurIPS. Published in main track at ICLR (no D&B track). |
| **AutoGen Studio** ([Wu et al., EMNLP 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15247)) | System Demo | The contribution is the no-code multi-agent prototyping tool with UI. Value is in the *software system*: drag-and-drop workflow composition, real-time debugging, profiling. Not a new agent algorithm. |
| **GPT-4 Technical Report** ([OpenAI, arXiv 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774)) | Research | The contribution is the model and its capabilities. GPT-4 introduces many benchmarks, but the *primary* value is the model itself and the empirical findings about scaling. |
| **DSPy** ([Khattab et al., ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03714)) | Research | The contribution is a programming paradigm (declarative LLM calls with optimized prompts). Though DSPy includes a framework, the intellectual contribution is the *algorithmic approach* to prompt optimization, not the software. |


### The Gray Zones: When Your Paper Could Go to Multiple Tracks

Not every paper falls neatly into one category. Here are the most common dilemmas and how to resolve them.

**"I built a new model AND a new benchmark to evaluate it."** This is by far the most common gray zone. The resolution depends on scale and intent. If the benchmark is large, independently valuable, and designed for community use (not just to evaluate your model), consider splitting into two papers: the model goes to the Research track, the benchmark goes to D&B. SWE-bench could have been split this way (the benchmark in one paper, SWE-agent in another), but the authors chose to present them together at ICLR. If the benchmark is small and designed purely as an evaluation tool for your specific method (e.g., you created 50 test examples to validate your approach), keep it in the Research paper. The benchmark isn't substantial enough for a standalone D&B submission.

**"I built a data collection tool AND used it to create a dataset."** Ask: which is the reusable contribution? If the *tool* is designed for general use by other researchers (configurable, documented, applicable to many domains), it may be a System Demo paper. This is what Fabricator ([Treachler et al., arXiv 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.09582)) did. It is a toolkit for LLM-assisted dataset generation, and the paper emphasizes the tool's architecture: modular classes, HuggingFace integration, workflow composability. If the *dataset* is the main contribution and the tool was just the mechanism you used to create it (a custom script that only works for your specific data domain), it is a D&B paper. Document the tool in the methodology section, but keep the spotlight on the data.

**"My dataset paper includes a novel algorithm for data cleaning."** If the data cleaning algorithm is *generalizable* (applicable to other datasets beyond the one you created), consider splitting. The algorithm goes to Research, the cleaned dataset goes to D&B. If the algorithm is specific to your dataset (e.g., a domain-specific heuristic for filtering noise in medical imaging data), keep it in the D&B paper as a *methodological contribution*. D&B papers absolutely can and should describe novel methodologies for data collection, annotation, and curation. What makes it a D&B paper rather than a Research paper is that the methodology is *in service of* the dataset, not the other way around.

**"I'm submitting to ACL or EMNLP, which don't have a separate D&B track."** At *CL venues, dataset and benchmark papers compete in the main track. This can feel disadvantageous. Your paper is being reviewed alongside algorithm papers by reviewers who might default to asking "Where is the algorithmic novelty?" However, both ACL and EMNLP have taken explicit steps to counteract this bias. The ARR reviewer guidelines state that "development of datasets is as important as modeling work" and that dataset papers should be evaluated on their own merits: quality, documentation, impact potential, and ethical considerations. The EMNLP 2025 CFP explicitly lists resource papers as a valid submission type and requires a Responsible NLP Checklist. If you submit a dataset paper to ACL/EMNLP, proactively address this in your introduction: frame your contribution using the "artifact contribution" language from the ARR guidelines, making it clear to reviewers that the paper's value is in the data artifact, not in algorithmic novelty.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: D&B papers are 'easier' to publish"}
Some researchers view the D&B track as a "back door" that is easier to get into than the main track, with lower standards. This is wrong. The NeurIPS D&B acceptance rate in 2022 was approximately 36%, which is comparable to the main track (~25–30% depending on the year). Moreover, the *type* of rigor demanded is different, not lower. Main track reviewers evaluate algorithmic novelty and experimental soundness. D&B track reviewers evaluate data quality, documentation completeness, accessibility, ethical sourcing, and community impact potential. Papers that would be strong in the main track can easily be rejected in D&B for insufficient documentation or inaccessible data. The standards are orthogonal, not hierarchical.
:::


### Dr. Chen's Decision: A Worked Walkthrough

Let us apply everything from this section to Dr. Chen's situation. She has three components:

**Component 1: The multilingual reasoning benchmark (15,000 questions, 40 languages)**

- *Primary contribution type:* Data artifact and evaluation infrastructure
- *Target track:* NeurIPS D&B track
- *Why:* The benchmark fills a specific gap. No existing benchmark evaluates multilingual reasoning at this scale and language coverage. The primary value is the *dataset and evaluation protocol*, not a new algorithm.
- *Key submission requirements:* Host on HuggingFace, provide Croissant metadata, run baselines with frontier models (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama), report inter-annotator agreement, document annotation methodology, address ethical considerations (especially cultural sensitivity in 40-language data collection).

**Component 2: The novel scoring algorithm**

- *Primary contribution type:* Algorithmic/methodological innovation
- *Target track:* NeurIPS main track or EMNLP main track
- *Why:* The value is the algorithm itself: a new metric that correlates better with human judgment. It should be evaluated on its *methodological* merits. Does it work? On how many tasks? How does it compare to existing metrics? The benchmark is a useful test bed, but the contribution is the metric.
- *Key submission requirements:* Double-blind, demonstrate correlation with human judgments on multiple datasets (not just her own benchmark), comparison with existing metrics (BLEU, BERTScore, etc.), ablation studies.

**Component 3: The Gradio annotation tool**

- *Primary contribution type:* Software system
- *Target track:* ACL or EMNLP System Demo track
- *Why:* The tool has independent value. Other researchers could use it for their own annotation campaigns. It has quality control dashboards, annotator management, real-time agreement monitoring. If it is general-purpose enough (configurable for different annotation tasks, not hard-coded for multilingual reasoning), it is a viable System Demo paper.
- *But:* If the tool is too specific to her particular annotation scheme and not easily reusable, it should be *described in the D&B paper* as part of the methodology section, not submitted separately. The System Demo bar is "would another research group download and use this tool?" If the answer is "maybe, but they'd have to modify it significantly," it is not ready for a standalone demo paper.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Does splitting your work into multiple papers feel like 'salami slicing'?"}
In some fields, breaking one study into multiple small papers is frowned upon as "least publishable unit" or "salami slicing." Is Mei's strategy of writing three papers from one project any different? The answer is yes, and the distinction is important. Salami slicing takes a *single coherent contribution* and artificially divides it into fragments that are individually incomplete. Mei's three components are *genuinely different types of contributions* that serve different communities and are evaluated by different criteria. The benchmark helps researchers who want to evaluate multilingual reasoning. The scoring algorithm helps researchers who need better evaluation metrics. The annotation tool helps researchers who need to run large-scale annotation campaigns. These are three different audiences, three different review processes, and three different sets of evaluation criteria. Submitting them separately is not fragmentation. It is routing each contribution to the audience that values it most. Moreover, each paper is complete on its own: the benchmark paper doesn't need the algorithm to be useful, and the algorithm paper doesn't need the tool to be understood.
:::

By the end of this analysis, Mei's path is clear. She will write a D&B paper for the benchmark (her strongest and most impactful contribution), a Research paper for the scoring algorithm (once she has validated it across multiple datasets), and *possibly* a System Demo paper for the annotation tool (if she generalizes it sufficiently). Far from diminishing any single contribution, this approach ensures that each piece of her work reaches the right audience, is reviewed by the right criteria, and can stand on its own merits. As we will see in the next two sections, writing a strong D&B paper (whether for a dataset or a benchmark) requires its own distinctive structure and set of skills.
